bp: A scientific citation is a small promise. When one paper cites another beside a claim, the reader is meant to believe that the cited work supports that claim, or at least belongs in the evidence trail behind it. The scholarly web is therefore not only a pile of papers. It is a network of claims, references, and inherited trust. Miscitation breaks that network: a reference may fail to support the local claim, or may even say the opposite. Manual checking cannot keep up with large citation graphs, but simple automated checks miss the point if they only ask whether two papers sound related. This paper serves editors, reviewers, database builders, and research readers who need scalable citation integrity checks. LAGMiD treats a citation as both text and position in a network, then uses language-model reasoning to teach a faster graph model how to detect unsupported or contradictory references.
wh: The hard part is that citation support is not the same as topic similarity. Two papers can use similar words because they study the same area, while one still does not support the specific sentence that cites it. The opposite can also happen: a paper may support a claim with different wording, so a surface match looks weak even though the citation is faithful. Network-only methods have a different blind spot. A strange citation pattern may be suspicious, but many bad citations sit in normal-looking neighborhoods because authors cite nearby work in expected ways. A full language model can read the local citation context and reason more deeply, but the abstract names two deployment problems: it can hallucinate and it is costly to run on large scholarly graphs. The central tension is therefore meaning versus scale: the system needs careful evidence checking without spending language-model effort on every citation.
naive: A smart beginner would take the sentence around a citation, take the abstract or text of the cited paper, measure how similar they are, and flag low similarity as suspicious. That catches some irrelevant references, but it confuses relatedness with support. A cited paper can be related to the topic yet contradict the citing claim. Another beginner would inspect the citation graph and flag unusual links, such as citations far outside a normal community. That also fails because a miscitation can be graph-normal: a paper can cite a nearby, popular, or methodologically related work in a way that still misstates what it shows. Both shortcuts avoid the harder question: does the cited evidence actually carry the claim?
ap: LAGMiD's core move is to use the expensive reasoner as a teacher and the cheaper graph learner as the everyday worker. For difficult citation cases, a large language model examines the citation context and traces evidence through multiple citation hops, asking how the local claim relates to the cited work and to surrounding papers. Those intermediate reasoning states are not thrown away after the language model gives an answer. They become supervision for a graph neural network, meaning a system that learns from nodes, links, and text attached to those nodes. Knowledge distillation here means compressing the teacher's richer checking behavior into the student model so later detections can run faster. A collaborative strategy then decides which cases should still be routed to the language model and which can be handled by the graph model using learned structure-based patterns.
mech: The mechanism begins with a text-rich citation graph. The nodes are scholarly papers. The links are citations. Around each link is a citation context: the local sentence or passage where one paper invokes another. First, LAGMiD asks a language model to perform evidence-chain reasoning. In plain terms, it does not judge a citation as an isolated pair only. It follows citation paths across several hops and checks whether the stated claim remains faithful to what the cited evidence and neighboring evidence say. Chain-of-thought prompting is used as an instruction style that asks the model to lay out intermediate steps, but the important object is the chain of evidence, not the label alone. Second, the system records intermediate reasoning states from that process. Third, it trains a graph neural network, a model that updates a paper's representation by mixing its own text with information from linked papers, so that the graph model's internal representations align with the language model's intermediate reasoning. Fourth, the trained graph model scores new citation cases cheaply by using citation structure plus text. Fifth, collaborative learning routes harder cases back to the language model while continuing to shape the graph model for broader generalization. The output is a miscitation decision or score that aims to preserve semantic checking while reducing repeated language-model calls.
math: The mathematics is built around three ordinary operations: comparing meaning, passing evidence through links, and compressing an expensive teacher into a cheaper student. Comparing meaning asks whether the claim near a citation and the cited evidence say compatible things. This is not just measuring shared words; it is a fidelity check, where the relation can be support, absence of support, or contradiction. Graph learning uses the citation network as a structure for moving evidence. A node is a paper, an edge is a citation, and a neighbor can provide context about how work is normally connected. This helps because a citation's meaning often depends on nearby papers and chains of prior support, but it can mislead when nearby papers are commonly cited for the wrong reason. Knowledge distillation is mathematical compression: a large teacher produces detailed intermediate signals, and a smaller student is trained to make its own internal numbers line up with those signals. The learning problem then defines what counts as wrong: not only a bad final miscitation label, but a graph-model representation that fails to match the teacher's reasoning states. The tradeoff is accuracy versus cost, with a second tradeoff between trusting language-model reasoning and guarding against hallucination.
dots: This paper sits where several recurring conference ideas meet. It belongs to citation integrity detection because the object being protected is the trust link between a scholarly claim and its reference. It also belongs to graph learning because the citation network is not decorative; links carry evidence about intellectual neighborhoods and multi-hop chains. It connects to ranking because the system must decide which citation cases deserve attention and, through collaborative routing, which cases are simple enough for the graph model and which need the language model. The repo's trust and misinformation family treats evidence management as the shared pressure behind videos, chatbot answers, sustainability claims, and scholarly references; LAGMiD is the scholarly version of that pressure. It is also close to retrieval and language-model papers that worry about whether cited sources really support generated answers. Across these neighbors, the same hidden problem appears: fluent or familiar evidence is not enough unless the support relation is checked.
ww: The approach should improve on the naive methods because it refuses to collapse citation checking into one weak signal. Similarity alone can tell that two texts live near the same topic, but it cannot reliably tell whether one supports a particular claim. Network anomaly alone can tell that a link looks unusual, but it cannot read what the author asserted. LAGMiD combines these views. The language model supplies a richer semantic check over local citation context and multi-hop evidence chains. The graph model supplies a scalable way to reuse repeated patterns across the scholarly network. Distillation matters because the graph model is not merely trained on final yes-or-no labels; it is pushed toward the intermediate shape of the teacher's reasoning, which should give it more useful internal distinctions. Collaborative routing adds a practical safety valve: routine cases can be handled cheaply, while complex cases can still receive deeper language-model reasoning. The method works if the teacher's reasoning states capture genuine citation support patterns and if those patterns repeat enough in graph structure and text for the student model to learn them.
po: The payoff is a citation-checking system that aims to combine careful semantic reasoning with large-scale operation. The abstract reports experiments on three real-world benchmarks and says LAGMiD achieves state-of-the-art miscitation detection with significantly reduced inference cost. In practical terms, that means the system is meant to catch references that fail to support or contradict local claims without asking a large language model to judge every citation from scratch. For scholarly databases, review tools, or research-assistance systems, the useful capability is triage: identify likely citation-integrity failures at a scale where manual reading alone would miss many cases.
limits: The claims depend on several assumptions the abstract cannot fully settle. The language model's evidence-chain reasoning must be mostly faithful; if it hallucinates support relations, distillation can teach the graph model the wrong habits. The citation graph must contain useful structure, because the graph model learns from links as well as text. If a field has systematic miscitation practices, normal graph neighborhoods may repeat the error instead of exposing it. The benchmarks show reported gains, but the abstract does not specify how well the method handles full papers versus abstracts, citation contexts outside the benchmark domains, adversarially written citations, or cases where support requires reading methods, tables, or negative results in detail.
